blurb: Sweet, dense, and deeply satisfying, kabocha brings color, texture, fiber, and natural sweetness to fall and winter meals.

blocks.text: How it fits the Protein Flip™

blocks.html: Kabocha does not need to be the protein on the plate to play an important nutritional role.

Its dense texture and natural sweetness make it a satisfying source of vegetables, fiber, and carbohydrate that can help build substance throughout the meal. From there, we can disperse protein around it with ingredients such as beans, lentils, seeds, yogurt, cheese, eggs, seafood, or a portion-smart primary protein.
That is the Protein Flip™ opportunity: instead of thinking of squash as simply a side dish next to a large piece of protein, use it as one of several ingredients working together to build the meal.

For example, roasted kabocha can become part of a bowl with lentils and toasted pumpkin seeds, sit alongside fish with a yogurt-herb sauce, or anchor a warm salad with greens, beans, and a little feta.

blocks.text: Technique: Roast it and let the squash do the work

blocks.html: Kabocha becomes especially good when roasted. The flesh turns creamy and almost chestnut-like while the edges caramelize.
Cut the squash in half, scoop out the seeds, then slice it into wedges or crescents. The skin is edible once cooked, so peeling is optional.
Toss lightly with olive oil, salt, and pepper and roast at 425°F until tender and browned around the edges, usually about 25 to 35 minutes, depending on the thickness of the pieces.

Because kabocha is naturally sweet, resist the instinct to add a sugary glaze right away. Roast it first and taste it. You may find that all it needs is acidity, spice, herbs, or a savory sauce to create contrast.

Think about these as starting points rather than fixed recipes. Once you understand what complements the squash, you can begin using what you already have in the kitchen.
Kabocha provides fiber along with carotenoid pigments, including beta-carotene, which give the flesh its deep orange color. It also brings satisfying carbohydrate and natural sweetness to a meal.

From a Protein Flip™ perspective, that matters because good nutrition does not have to come from one dominant ingredient. The squash contributes its part, while proteins, vegetables, seeds, sauces, and other components contribute theirs.
The result is a meal where nutrition is dispersed across the plate rather than asking one oversized protein to do all the work.
